items.prompt: I’m going to show you how to decide whether two fractions are equivalent.  20/12  5/4  The fractions are equivalent if this is equal to one. My turn first. Five times what is twenty?

My turn again. The fractions are equivalent if this is equal to one. Five times what is twenty?
Three times what is twelve?
items.demo: Three times four is twelve.  20/12 = 5/3 × 4/4  Top and bottom are the same, so this is equal to one. The fractions are *equivalent*.

items.prompt: First, look for a whole-number multiplier between the top numbers. If there is one, check whether the same multiplier connects the bottom numbers. If there is no whole-number multiplier, we need another way to check. For 20/12 and 6/3, compare the cross-products: twenty times three and six times twelve.
items.demo: 20 × 3 = 60, while 6 × 12 = 72. The cross-products differ, so these fractions are *not equivalent*.

items.prompt: Fractions can be equivalent even when their top numbers are not in each other’s whole-number times tables. For example, 6/9 and 4/6.
items.demo: Both fractions simplify to *2/3*, so they are equivalent. Their cross-products also match: 6 × 6 = 36 and 4 × 9 = 36.
